newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Pick 'n Pay unveils financial services plan.
newsitem.headline: Pick 'n Pay unveils financial services plan.

text.p: Supermarket giant Pick 'n Pay Stores Ltd on Tuesday unveiled details of its plan to provide a range of financial services from early September.

Head of its new financial services division Gareth Ackerman said that as from September 10, its first financial services product, the Cash Account, would be officially available but that other developments were in the pipeline.

Both a savings and a transmission account, the Cash Account will offer higher interest rates and lower services charges than the commercial banks and is expected to sign up 100,000 customers within the first year.

On balances of up to 999 rand, it will pay five percent interest while balances between 1,000 and 1,999 rand will get eight percent, 2,000 to 9,999 rand 10 percent, 10,000 to 14,999 rand 14 percent and more than 15,000 rand 14.75 percent. The minimum balance is 10 rand.

"Depending on the balance maintained in the account, Pick and Pay will effectively offer interest rates comparable with those offered on 32-day call accounts, with the advantage that funds are instantly available," Ackerman said.
Service charges will be between 20 and 30 percent cheaper than those charged by commercial banks.

Ackerman said that Pick 'n Pay had been able to offer the higher interest rates because it did not have the heavy infrastructural costs carried by the commercial banks and would take a lower profit margin.
The Cash Account would be backed by Boland Bank, which indicated that Pick 'n Pay was not planning to compete for the customer base of the large commercial banks, he said.
"The service is being introduced in the Western Cape but will be extended to all stores, covering 3,500 checkouts nationally by the end of the year," Ackerman said.

Customers would be able to make deposits and withdrawals at check-outs, pay for their purchases, transfer funds from one account to another, pay their rates, telephone and electricity bills and make regular payments on a stop order basis.
Alternatively, they could do their banking telephonically through a newly-built Call Centre in Claremont in the Western Cape.

Ackerman said that the major difference between the Cash Account and more familiar credit card was that it was a debit card, thus avoiding the danger of bed debts while allowing customers to pay for their purchases without having to draw cash.
This was seen as a major attraction of the Cash Account as many people did not like drawing large sums of money before going shopping.

Ackerman said that the group had conducted extensive research into the project over the last year, consulting with other projects such as the UK's Sainsbury's Bank, a joint venture with the Bank of Scotland.

Pick 'n Pay Financial Services managing director Nicky Bicket said the next phase would be to provide a banking service on the Internet by the end of the year. A marketing website would be launched shortly.
